extracted.intended_audience: named correspondents (Le Roy, Washington, Madison, Monroe, Carmichael) and educated statesmen/scientific peers
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Thomas Jefferson's private and public letters (late 1786) discussing natural philosophy (sea breezes, winds), commercial/administrative affairs, and political organization; the text contains advice, prescriptions, and evaluative remarks directed to specific correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for a merchant partner
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill, punctuality, and integrity are the requisites in such a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: In recommending a merchant to head an American branch of a large fur-trade company, Jefferson states that the important qualities in the person are skill, punctuality, and integrity; the half of the company resident in America should supervise details while the other half may make advances. Use these three virtues as primary selection criteria when recommending or choosing an agent/partner for major trade undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and correction of facts in published articles
rubrics_metrics.description: It is material to set facts to rights, as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: On revising the 'Etats Unis' article for the Encyclopédie Méthodique, Jefferson criticizes the author's ignorance and bias, rewrote the article, and sent corrections. Principle: authors and editors should prioritize factual accuracy, correct errors, avoid inserting unsupported opinions or partisan philippics, and welcome corrections from informed readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and distribution of governmental powers
rubrics_metrics.description: To make us one nation as to foreign concerns, and keep us distinct in domestic ones, gives the outline of the proper division of powers between the general and particular governments. The first and last [legislative and judiciary] are already separated. The second [executive] should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson's proposal: organize government into three separate departments (legislative, executive, judiciary); impose separation of the executive (e.g., create a standing executive committee during Congress recesses and a receiving/dispatching committee during sessions) so Congress handles principally legislative business. Use separation of powers and imposed structural rules if representative bodies will not self-limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper size and division of western states for governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A tractable people may be governed in large bodies: but in proportion as they depart from this character, the extent of their government must be less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson argues that making western states fewer and larger reverses the 'natural order of things'—smaller political divisions are preferable for populations that are not uniformly tractable; improper sizing risks severance of western parts of the confederacy. Use governability and local character as criteria when determining political subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification for a judicial appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: The [judiciary] would require a little previous drudgery at the bar, to qualify you to discharge your duty with satisfaction to yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson advises that prior practical experience at the bar is necessary before accepting a judiciary seat; treat hands-on legal practice as a qualification requirement for judicial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of heating air and their role in sea breezes
rubrics_metrics.description: Air resting on a heated and reflecting surface becomes warmer, rarer, and lighter: it ascends therefore, and the circumjacent air, which is colder and heavier, flows into its place... The air, then, is warmed, 1. by the direct rays of the sun; 2. by its reflected rays; 3. by contact with the heated surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson lays out three mechanisms by which ground heats the air and drives local circulations. Apply these factors (direct radiation, reflection, and conduction/contact) to evaluate where and when sea breezes develop; note that surface properties (forest vs cultivated land, opaque vs pellucid medium) alter these modes and therefore breeze strength and penetration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forest and sea reduce atmospheric heating (anti-heating factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A forest ... reflects upwards [sun rays] intercepted by leaves; leaves inclined towards the horizon reflect the rays downwards. These leaves having a power of keeping themselves cool by their own transpiration, they impart no heat to the air by contact. ... The sea being pellucid ... its surface, therefore, is comparatively cool, for these reasons; to which may be added that of evaporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of forest cover (interception, transpiration) and the sea's translucency and mixing (diffusion of heat and evaporation) as criteria predicting cooler overlying air and thus weaker or absent local heating-driven breezes compared to cultivated opaque land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountainous and forested barriers to sea-breeze penetration (enumerated reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are circumstances which render it possible that [sea breezes] may not be able to pass those intermediate mountains. 1. These mountains constitute the highest lands ... The air on them must consequently be very cold and heavy, and have a tendency to flow both to the east and west. 2. Ranging across the current of the sea breezes, they are in themselves, so many successive barriers opposed to their progress. 3. The country they occupy is covered with trees, which assist to weaken and spend the force of the breezes. 4. It will remain so covered; a very small proportion of it being capable of culture. 5. The temperature of its air, then, will never be softened by culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these five specific factors when assessing whether coastal sea-breeze systems can penetrate inland across mountain ranges: altitude and cold dense air, barrier alignment across current, forest cover weakening winds, lack of cultivable land preventing future weakening, and persistently cold unsmoothed air temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing institutional risk of hereditary aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every writing ... considers [the Society of Cincinnati] as dishonorable and destructive to our governments; ... the germ whose developement is one day to destroy the fabric we have reared. ... though the day may be at some distance ... yet it will certainly come, when a single fibre left of this institution will produce an hereditary aristocracy, which will change the form of our governments from the best to the worst in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson uses as an evaluative test whether an institution contains structures or 'germs' that could lead to hereditary privilege or aristocracy; if so, it should be eradicated. Use potential for creating entrenched hereditary power as a criterion when judging societies/institutions in a republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicted consequences of opening an isthmian passage (Panama) to tropical currents
rubrics_metrics.description: Were they to make an opening through the Isthmus of Panama, ... the tropical current entering it with all its force, would soon widen it ... These consequences would follow. 1. Vessels ... would have a steady wind and tide ... thus performing with speed and safety the tour of the whole globe, to within about twenty-four degrees of longitude. 2. The Gulf of Mexico ... would become stagnant and safe. 3. The Gulf Stream on the coast of the United States would cease, and with that, those derangements of course and reckoning, which now impede and endanger the intercourse with those States. 4. The fogs on the Banks of Newfoundland ... would disappear. 5. Those Banks ... it might become problematical what effect changes of pasture and temperatures would have on the fisheries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jefferson sets out an explicit set of five predicted maritime/climatic and navigational consequences if a permanent passage were opened through Panama; use these listed outcomes as criteria for evaluating the broader environmental and navigational impacts of major interoceanic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficiency metric for steam-mills vs horses
rubrics_metrics.description: Six horses ... will grind six bushels of flour in an hour ... They can work thus six hours in the twenty-four, grinding thirty-six bushels ... His steam-mill ... consumes one hundred and twenty bushels of coal in twenty-four hours, turns ten pair of stones, which grind eight bushels of flour an hour each, which is nineteen hundred and twenty bushels in the twenty-four hours. This makes a peck and a half of coal perform exactly as much as a horse in one day can perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct output and fuel/consumption comparisons (bushels ground per day per power source; coal consumption per output) as a practical metric to evaluate mechanization efficiency. Jefferson reports Boulton's empirical numbers showing large advantage to steam in continuous work capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly humility and marking conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: We know too little of the operations of nature in the physical world, to assign causes with any degree of confidence. Willing always, however, to guess at what we do not know, I have sometimes indulged myself with conjectures on the causes of the phenomena above stated. I will hazard them on paper, for your amusement, premising for their foundation some principles believed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When offering scientific hypotheses in absence of conclusive evidence, explicitly flag them as conjectures, state foundational principles on which they rest, and present them cautiously for critique and amusement rather than as definitive claims.
